advanced-industries.overview: Advanced industries covers engineering-heavy manufacturers: carmakers and their suppliers, aircraft and defense companies, and makers of industrial machinery and equipment. Products take years to design and depend on long, global supply chains, so these companies are shaped by how full their factories are, trade policy and the cost of materials like steel. A large share of their profit often comes from servicing and spare parts after the original sale.
advanced-industries.recap: Aerospace and defense stayed strong: GE Aerospace's orders jumped 49%, RTX's backlog reached $340 billion and Northrop Grumman's backlog hit a record $110 billion, and all three raised their outlooks. GM beat on North American trucks and added a $20 billion buyback. 3M raised its profit outlook and signed a data center optics deal with Amazon. Tesla's revenue was flat at $28 billion while operating profit fell 56% as AI and robot spending outran gross profit.

consumer-retail.overview: Consumer and retail covers the companies that make and sell what people buy day to day. That includes stores and online retailers, makers of food, drinks and household products, farm and food businesses, and travel and hospitality companies like airlines and hotels. Consumer spending is about two-thirds of the US economy, so these businesses rise and fall with how confident people feel and how much money they have left after essentials.
consumer-retail.recap: Fuel costs were the common thread. US airlines' fuel spending rose 55% to 67% while revenue rose 16% to 22%, and Southwest's fuel bill rose $821 million with $4.55 a gallon planned for the fourth quarter. P&G grew sales 4% to $23.3 billion and held its outlook despite higher oil-linked costs, and S&P Global warned the Hormuz energy shock could become a food crisis in 2027. Silgan and American Industrial Partners agreed to buy Trivium Packaging for $3.4 billion.

energy-materials.overview: Energy and materials covers the companies that pull resources out of the ground and turn them into fuel, power and raw materials. That includes oil and gas producers, the pipelines, ships and terminals that move their output, refineries and chemical plants, electric utilities and renewable developers, and miners and steelmakers. These are capital-heavy businesses that live with commodity prices they don't control, so returns depend on keeping costs low and investing at the right point in the cycle.
energy-materials.recap: Hormuz kept oil high all week: Brent held near $110 to $112 as Iran said it attacked ships, and on Friday US crude rose 3.8% to $103.27 after new Iranian warnings. Gas is tight too, with Asian LNG at a near four-year high and Europe entering winter with low storage while Qatar's LNG capacity stays partly offline. Halliburton's North America revenue slipped despite high prices while its international work grew. In power, Microsoft signed a 20-year Indiana supply deal with NiSource and Bloom Energy's revenue more than doubled to a record $1.24 billion. Steelmakers posted strong volumes, with Steel Dynamics shipping a record 3.78 million tons.

financial-services.overview: Financial services is the business of managing, lending, investing and moving money. Banks take deposits and make loans, insurers collect premiums to cover risks, asset managers invest on behalf of savers and pension funds, and payments companies handle the flow of money between people and businesses. It is one of the most heavily regulated industries, so how much capital firms must hold and how well they control risk shapes how profitable they can be.
financial-services.recap: Deals and penalties led the week. Bank of America faced $1.2 billion in penalties over anti-money-laundering failures, LSEG agreed to buy Octus for more than $3.5 billion, Dai-ichi Life approached Challenger with an A$7.9 billion offer, and Tradeweb agreed to buy Trumid for about $1.97 billion. Stablecoin payments rose 45% this year as Visa, Mastercard and Stripe link crypto to cards. W. R. Berkley's premium growth slowed to 1%. American Express posted record quarterly revenue of $20.1 billion and raised its profit outlook, then announced a 5% job cut.

healthcare.overview: Healthcare covers the companies that discover, make, pay for and deliver medical care. Drugmakers and biotech firms develop medicines, device makers build everything from surgical tools to heart implants, insurers pay for care, and hospitals and doctors provide it. In the US the system is large and complex, and prices are set through negotiation between manufacturers, insurers and the middlemen between them, so policy and regulation matter as much as science.
healthcare.recap: Drug and device companies mostly reported solid quarters: J&J raised its profit forecast and is weighing an orthopedics spinoff, Thermo Fisher's revenue grew 9% to $12.14 billion, Quest Diagnostics grew revenue 10% to $3.10 billion and Intuitive Surgical's procedures grew 15%. Moderna fell about 18% after melanoma vaccine data leaked early, showing a 42% cut in recurrence or death risk. Merck KGaA agreed to buy Silence Therapeutics for $1.3 billion, and EQT agreed to take QIAGEN private for $12.1 billion. CMS proposed flat fees for drug middlemen in Medicare Part D.

infrastructure-logistics.overview: Infrastructure and logistics covers the physical networks the rest of the economy runs on. That includes the trucking, rail, shipping and air freight companies that move goods, the developers and builders behind homes, offices and data centers, and the public sector that funds and regulates much of it. These businesses are sensitive to fuel costs and interest rates, because moving goods burns diesel and most buildings are paid for with borrowed money.
infrastructure-logistics.recap: Higher costs and rates weighed on the sector. Diesel near $6.30 spread fuel surcharges through supply chains, homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest since 2012 with mortgage rates near 7.4%, and the 10-year yield above 5% pressured REITs. Union Pacific posted record third-quarter results with revenue up 15% while its Norfolk Southern merger stays under review. EQT agreed to buy Cleanaway for about A$9.3 billion, and Maximus agreed to buy defense contractor Agile Defense for $660 million.

macro.overview: The macro picture covers the forces that move every industry at once: how fast economies are growing, how quickly prices are rising, where central banks set interest rates, and how goods and money flow between countries. When energy costs climb or borrowing gets more expensive, the effects show up in nearly every company's results, so this is the backdrop for reading the rest of the news.
macro.recap: Energy and interest rates drove the week. Brent held near $110 to $112 on Hormuz disruption, and on Friday US crude rose to $103.27, up 14% for October. The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.00% on Friday after touching 5.15% earlier in the week, and the Fed ends its meeting on Wednesday, expected to hold rates. China grew 4.5% in the third quarter on exports while consumers and property stayed weak, and Canada's inflation rose to 3.1% on a 28% jump in gasoline prices. The Nasdaq fell 2.6% on Thursday on doubts about AI spending.

tmt.overview: Tech, media and telecom covers the companies behind computing and communication: chipmakers, software and cloud providers, internet platforms like search and social media, entertainment and streaming companies, and the telecom networks that connect everything. Many of these businesses become more profitable as they grow, because serving one more customer costs very little, which is why a handful of very large companies dominate. Much of the sector's investment today is going into the data centers and chips that power AI.
tmt.recap: Doubts about AI spending hit tech: Meta grew revenue 26% to $64.6 billion but its free cash flow turned negative on capital spending of $135 to $145 billion this year, and the Nasdaq fell 2.6% on Thursday. Deals continued, with Salesforce agreeing to buy Braze for $5.66 billion, Proofpoint buying Varonis for $6.3 billion and Bumble going private for $1.3 billion. SpaceX grew revenue 161% to $14.6 billion in its first full public quarter, and Texas Instruments revenue rose 28% to $6.06 billion. Netflix guided to a lower margin and is cutting about 1,000 jobs, and Comcast lost 144,000 broadband customers while adding 368,000 wireless lines.

aerospace-defense.operatingModel: Engine and systems makers often sell original equipment near cost and earn high margins on decades of spare parts and services. Defense primes earn steady but capped margins (often about 10%) on government contracts, with large backlogs giving visibility.
aerospace-defense.overview: Aerospace and defense covers makers of commercial aircraft, jet engines and aircraft systems, and suppliers of military equipment such as missiles, fighter jets and ships. Commercial aerospace sells to airlines and earns much of its profit from long-term aftermarket service, while defense sells mostly to governments under multi-year contracts. Both rely on deep, specialized supply chains with few qualified suppliers.
players: Aircraft makers: Boeing and Airbus (a duopoly), plus Embraer and COMAC
Engine makers: GE Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney (RTX), Rolls-Royce, Safran
Defense primes: Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, BAE Systems
Structure: concentrated at the top, with high barriers from certification and security rules
threats: Supply chain failures and quality problems
Airline bankruptcies when fuel prices spike
trends: Aircraft deliveries lag demand, so airlines fly older planes longer and aftermarket service booms
Defense budgets are rising in Europe, the Middle East and Asia after wars in Ukraine and the Gulf
Munitions and air defense restocking is creating multi-year backlogs
Supply chain bottlenecks in castings, forgings and engines cap output
Consolidation among suppliers to secure scarce capacity

agriculture-food.overview: Agriculture and food covers the chain from farm inputs (seeds, fertilizer, crop protection, machinery) through farming and grain trading to food processing. Farmers sell crops and livestock at commodity prices they do not control, so their profits depend on input costs, weather and global trade. telecom.operatingModel: Operators earn recurring subscription revenue with EBITDA margins of roughly 30-40%, but must reinvest about 15-20% of revenue every year in networks. Profit depends on keeping churn low and filling the network with more paying customers.
telecom.overview: Telecom companies build and run networks that carry voice and data, selling mobile, broadband and TV subscriptions to consumers and connectivity to businesses. They spend heavily on spectrum licenses, towers and fiber, then recover that investment through monthly fees from millions of customers. Most markets have three or four main operators, and regulators control spectrum and mergers.
players: US: Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile US
Europe: Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone, Orange, Telefonica
Asia: China Mobile, NTT, Reliance Jio
Structure: 3-4 operators per country in a regulated oligopoly
threats: High debt and rising interest rates
trends: Satellite-to-phone services (SpaceX Starlink and others) threaten coverage advantages
Fiber broadband buildouts and fixed-wireless competition
Pressure in Europe to allow mergers and reduce the number of operators
Selling towers and fiber to infrastructure funds to cut debt
Flat revenue per user and price competition

marketSize.globalNote: Global logistics market (est., 2025)
marketSize.usNote: US business logistics costs, about 8% of GDP (CSCMP State of Logistics, 2024 approx.)

transport-logistics.operatingModel: Asset-heavy carriers earn revenue per mile or per container and live on utilization. Contract rates are set annually while spot rates swing daily; fuel surcharges pass part of fuel cost to shippers with a lag. Brokers are asset-light and earn the spread between shipper and carrier rates.
transport-logistics.overview: Moving goods and people: trucking, rail, parcel, ocean shipping, air cargo, airlines and the freight brokers in between.
players: Parcel: UPS, FedEx, Amazon Logistics
Rail: Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern
Ocean: Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM, COSCO
Trucking and brokerage: J.B. Hunt, Knight-Swift, C.H. Robinson
Highly fragmented trucking: most US carriers run fewer than 10 trucks
threats: Labor disputes at ports and rail
trends: Diesel near $6.30 is pushing fuel surcharges through supply chains
Shipping rerouted away from Hormuz and the Red Sea, raising freight and insurance rates
Truckers on fixed contracts are losing money; capacity may exit
Nearshoring to Mexico is lifting cross-border freight
Automation in warehouses and autonomous trucking pilots

marketSize.globalNote: Global airline revenue, IATA forecast for 2026 (made December 2025); hotels, cruises and bookings are additional
marketSize.usNote: US airline revenue, approx. (from memory, 2024-25)

travel-hospitality.operatingModel: Airlines earn revenue from tickets, bags and loyalty programs but carry heavy fixed costs, so a few percentage points of seats filled decide profit. Hotel brands mostly collect fees from franchisees and owners and take little operating risk.
travel-hospitality.overview: Travel and hospitality covers the airlines, hotels, cruise lines, rental firms and booking sites that move and host people on trips. Costs are mostly fixed (planes, buildings, crews), so profit swings sharply with how full they are and with fuel and labor costs. Leisure and business travel recover at different speeds after shocks, and demand follows consumer confidence.
players: Airlines: Delta, United, American, Southwest; Ryanair, Lufthansa, Emirates
Hotels: Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt; Airbnb; Booking Holdings and Expedia
Structure: a few big US airlines run most of the market; hotels are brand franchisors
threats: Fuel price spikes and conflict-related airspace closures
Recession reducing business and leisure travel
trends: Jet fuel at about $152 a barrel in 2026 versus $90 in 2025 is cutting airline profits
Premium cabins and loyalty programs earn a growing share of airline profit
Record passenger numbers, about 5.2 billion expected in 2026
Aircraft and engine shortages limit how fast airlines can add capacity
Hotel chains lean on franchising and fees instead of owning buildings
Travel demand is split: wealthier travelers keep spending while lower-income ones trade down
